p159.lead: Four weeks of mission in the Decapolis without a single miracle: the sermon on forgiveness, the strange preacher, principles for teachers, how to read the Scriptures, and positive religion.

p159.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p159.s0.h: Introduction — A Mission in Twelve Groups
p159.s0.b0: At Magadan Park nearly one hundred evangelists and disciples, including the women’s corps, were waiting to begin the Decapolis tour. On August 18 Jesus paired each apostle with one of the twelve evangelists and sent them out, with the other evangelists, in twelve groups. The tour was to last four weeks, and Jesus promised to visit them often during that time.
p159.s0.b1: They labored in Gerasa, Gamala, Hippos, Gadara, Philadelphia, Scythopolis, and many other cities. The text states plainly that throughout this tour there were no miracles of healing or other extraordinary events. What the paper leaves us is not wonders but the teachings Jesus gave as he visited each group.

head: Place visited
Apostle there
Theme of the teaching
rows: Hippos
Simon Peter
Forgiveness — the lost sheep and the unforgiving steward
Gamala
John

p159.s1.h: I. The Sermon on Forgiveness — The Father Who Goes Out First
p159.s1.b0: At Hippos Jesus taught forgiveness with the story of the shepherd who leaves the ninety and nine to search for the one sheep that has gone astray. He summed up in a single sentence the difference between the older religion and the gospel of the kingdom.
p159.s1.b2: Because the Father forgives us, we must learn to forgive one another. Jesus set out concrete steps to follow when a brother does wrong. The fellowship cannot judge souls or forgive sins, but it has been entrusted with maintaining temporal order on earth.

head: Step
What to do
rows: Go to him and, with tact and patience, show him his fault between the two of you alone
If he will not listen, go again, taking one or two mutual friends
If he still refuses, tell the whole story to the congregation
If he refuses to hear the brotherhood, let them take such action as they deem wise

p159.s1.b4: When Peter asked whether forgiving seven times was enough, Jesus answered “⟦Q 159:1.4⟧seventy times and seven⟦/Q⟧” and told the parable of the unforgiving steward: a man forgiven ten thousand talents threw into prison a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii.
p159.s1.b6: The text concludes that Jesus taught the dangers and unfairness of sitting in personal judgment on others. Legislative and judicial authority was vested in the group, not the individual, and even then was not to be exercised as personal authority, because an individual’s verdict is easily warped by prejudice or passion. For those of us who deal with conflict in a community today, this principle holds just as firmly.
p159.s2.h: II. The Strange Preacher — Whoever Is Not Against Us
p159.s2.b0: At Gamala John reported that he had forbidden a man who was teaching in Jesus’ name and casting out devils, because the man had never been with them. Jesus told him not to forbid such a one, and to rejoice that their teaching had begun to spread beyond the bounds of their personal influence.
p159.s2.b2: John felt this contradicted Jesus’ earlier saying, “⟦Q 159:2.2⟧He who is not with me is against me⟦/Q⟧.” The text explains that the earlier saying concerned an individual’s personal relation to the spiritual teachings of the kingdom, while this one concerned administrative jurisdiction among groups of believers. The man, whose name was Aden, ignored the prohibition, went on with his work, and raised up a considerable company of believers at Kanata. The lesson to rejoice in good work outside one’s own circle rather than to guard against it is all the more needed in a day of many denominations and organizations.
p159.s3.h: III. Instruction for Teachers and Believers — Respect the Personality
p159.s3.b0: At Edrei Jesus taught the principles that should guide those who proclaim truth. The text presents them summarized and restated in modern phraseology. At their heart is respect for human personality and the conviction that spiritual victories are won only by spiritual power.

head: Avoid
Do instead
rows: Coercing by overpowering argument, mental superiority, or shrewd eloquence
Appeal directly to the divine spirit dwelling within the mind
Appealing to fear, pity, or mere sentiment
Be fair and restrained, respecting the personality of your pupils
Destroying self-respect; condemning only the wrongs
Give generous recognition to what is praiseworthy
Sarcasm and cynicism toward the timid
Help them find work and escape idleness
Frightening people into the kingdom
Lead as a loving father does, without fear
False sympathy that feeds self-pity
Offer sympathy to the brave

p159.s3.b2: Jesus warned that strong feelings of emotion are not the same as the leadings of the divine spirit. Everyone who passes from the life of the flesh to the life of the spirit must cross a fringe of conflict, and all experience some uncertainty in that time of transition. Yet the gospel yoke is easy and the burden of truth is light.
p159.s3.b4: The teaching on self-respect is finely balanced. Too much self-respect ends in pride, and the loss of it often ends in paralysis of the will. So the gospel restores self-respect to those who have lost it and restrains it in those who have it. This principle—build up a person’s dignity first when you hope to help him change—applies equally at home and in the classroom.
p159.s3.b6: He told them not to portray him as a man of sorrows. Those who accept this teaching are filled with joy, and the happiness of those who are certain about God keeps growing. He also said that faith does not make us immune to calamity but makes us unafraid when it comes. For those who mistake faith for a guarantee against trouble, this distinction is essential.
p159.s3.b8: Jesus asked them to make known that he is tender of his children’s feelings and patient with their frailties, but ruthless with sin and intolerant of iniquity. Gentleness and firmness are not at odds. This balance—generous toward people, uncompromising toward evil—is the pattern a teacher should follow. He added that a faith assured of the divine presence expands the mind, reinforces the personality, and enhances the power to love and be loved.
p159.s4.h: IV. The Talk with Nathaniel — How to See the Scriptures
p159.s4.b0: At Abila Nathaniel, troubled that Jesus seemed to detract from the authority of the Scriptures, took him aside to ask. Jesus asked him not yet to share the answer with his brethren, and said that he did not regard the Scriptures as the rabbis did. They are the work of men and reflect the views and enlightenment of the times in which they arose.

head: The Scriptures as Jesus saw them
In brief
rows: Origin
Altogether human and faulty; only recently gathered as we now have them
Value
The best collection of religious wisdom and spiritual truth to be found at this time
Ground of their sacredness
They show the thoughts and acts of men who sought to find God
Limits
Much in them misrepresents the loving Father
Purpose
Religious instruction and spiritual guidance — not history or philosophy
Most deplorable
The idea of absolute perfection and infallibility, and the misinterpretation of the scribes

p159.s4.b3: Jesus said that the authority of truth is the very spirit dwelling in its living manifestations, not the dead words of men of another generation. He made no written record of the gospel lest, after he was gone, his followers divide into contending groups over differing interpretations. Nathaniel was enlightened but also shocked, and he told no one of this talk until after the ascension. To honor scripture without making an idol of it remains a task for every believer.
p159.s5.h: V. The Positive Nature of Jesus’ Religion — Overcome Evil with Good
p159.s5.b0: At Philadelphia James asked how to choose the better passages of Scripture, and Jesus pointed to teachings about a clean heart, the Lord as shepherd, love of neighbor, the promise to fear not, and nations learning war no more. He took the best of the Jewish religion and set it in the gospel, making the fatherhood of God the cornerstone and the practice of the brotherhood of man imperative.
p159.s5.b1: Jesus called for positive action instead of negative compliance. Turning the other cheek did not mean standing there dumb and passive, but actively doing the best thing possible to lead an erring brother into better ways. He taught three ways of contending with evil.

head: Method
Character
rows: Return evil for evil
Positive but unrighteous
Suffer evil without complaint and without resistance
Purely negative
Return good for evil; become master of the situation; overcome evil with good
Positive and righteous

p159.s5.b4: If forced to carry a stranger’s pack, do not sit and sigh while berating him under your breath; if nothing better comes to mind, carry it a second mile. Jesus turned the negative golden rule into a positive admonition, and through everyday words like salt, leaven, and little children he brought the philosophy of religion down from heaven to earth. His call to take the initiative and turn a situation toward good, rather than merely endure harm, offers a third way between passive resignation and retaliation.
p159.s6.h: VI. The Return to Magadan — The Last Rest
p159.s6.b0: The four-week mission was moderately successful, and hundreds were received into the kingdom. Above all, the apostles and evangelists gained the valuable experience of carrying on the work without Jesus’ immediate presence. On September 16 everyone gathered at Magadan, and David’s messengers brought reports from all over Palestine.
p159.s6.b1: The text singles out the value of the messenger corps. They kept the believers in touch with each other and with Jesus, and in these dark days they collected funds to support the families of the apostles and evangelists. David maintained an overnight relay service between Jerusalem and Bethsaida. The week that followed was their last rest, for the Perean mission would become an unbroken campaign of preaching and teaching all the way to Jerusalem. That the labor of unnamed helpers behind the scenes sustains a whole community is just as true of our gatherings today.
p159.s7.b0: Paper 159 contains not a single miracle. Instead it is full of mature teaching on forgiveness, tolerance, the attitude of a teacher, how to read scripture, and how to resist evil. Jesus’ religion was not a list of things not to do but an invitation to do good actively.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Take the first step toward reconciliation
The Father goes forth first to find them (159:1.2)
Forgive as generously as you have been forgiven
Freely received, freely give (159:1.5)
Rejoice in the good work of other groups
He who is not against us is for us (159:2.1)
When persuading, guard the other’s personality and self-respect
Respect the personality (159:3.2, 159:3.3)
Honor scripture without making it an idol of infallibility
Nothing human nature has touched (159:4.8)
Walk the second mile when wronged
Overcome evil with good (159:5.14, 159:5.15)

p159.s7.b2: In the next paper, Paper 160, “Rodan of Alexandria,” the Greek philosopher Rodan sets forth Jesus’ teachings for the apostles as a philosophy of living.
p160.lead: The Greek philosopher Rodan weaves Jesus’ gospel together with his own philosophy into an art of living: maturity, friendship, the rest of worship, the art of defeat, and the religion of the ideal.

p160.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p160.s0.h: Introduction — A Philosopher Meets the Gospel
p160.s0.b0: On September 18, after the Decapolis mission, most of the apostles went home for a week and Jesus enjoyed almost complete rest. Meanwhile Nathaniel and Thomas were busy in discussion with Rodan, a Greek philosopher from Alexandria. Rodan had become a disciple through the mission of one of Abner’s associates and was working to harmonize his philosophy of life with Jesus’ teachings.
p160.s0.b1: Jesus declined to enter the discussion himself but told the two apostles to listen to all Rodan had to say and to tell him about the gospel in return. Rodan gave ten addresses to some two dozen people, and this paper presents them condensed and restated in modern phraseology. We should therefore read these words not as Jesus’ own teaching but as the reflections of a philosopher who had embraced the gospel.
p160.s1.h: I. Rodan’s Greek Philosophy — Maturity and Problem Solving
p160.s1.b0: Rodan saw human life as made up of three great drives: urges, desires, and lures. Strong character is acquired by raising each of these to a higher level.

head: Drive of life
What strong character does with it
rows: Urges
Converts the natural urge of life into the social art of living
Desires
Transforms present desires into higher longings capable of lasting attainment
Lures
Transfers them from conventional ideas to unexplored ideas and undiscovered ideals

p160.s1.b2: The more complex civilization becomes, the harder the art of living, and mankind must learn it anew every ten generations—perhaps every generation. Animals make no inquiry into the purpose of life, but man not only grasps meanings; he is conscious of the meaning of meanings. Rodan named discouragement, worry, and indolence as evidence of moral immaturity, and said that mature people view the immature with the love parents bear their children.
p160.s1.b3: Rodan explained social maturity by the same principle. A society’s maturity shows in how far it gives up present desires in pursuit of permanent goals. Beyond that, its true badge is the willingness to leave the ease of established beliefs to pursue undiscovered ideals. Between the comfort of familiar ideas and the discomfort of seeking new truth, maturity always chooses the latter.
p160.s1.b4: The first step in solving any problem is to locate the difficulty and frankly acknowledge it. Yet when a problem stirs our fears or requires us to give up conceit and prejudice, people prefer to cling to old illusions. Beyond this, one also needs the tact and tolerance that win the cooperation of others.
p160.s1.b6: The greatest method of problem solving Rodan had learned from Jesus was the habit of withdrawing alone for worshipful meditation. It gives not only strength for everyday conflicts but energy for solving moral and spiritual problems. He added that prejudice is bound up with selfishness and disappears through devotion to a cause greater than oneself.
p160.s2.h: II. The Art of Living — What Friendship and Marriage Give
p160.s2.b0: What distinguishes man from the animal is the ability to communicate meanings, values, and ideals through symbols. This ability develops personality and gives rise to culture and civilization. The most effective social group is the family, and personal affection is the spiritual bond that holds it together. Rodan said that relationships of friendship and mutual affection contribute four things to the art of living.

head: What friendship gives
Rodan’s explanation
rows: Mutual self-expression and self-understanding
Noble impulses die with no one to hear them; recognition and appreciation are essential to character
Union of souls — the mobilization of wisdom
Pooling insight guards against prejudice and narrowness; the reason the Master always sent them two and two
Enthusiasm for living
Isolation drains the soul’s energy; friendship adds joy and stirs the imagination
Enhanced defense against evil
Troubles weigh more when borne alone; association greatly lessens suffering

p160.s2.b3: Rodan said he did not hesitate to glorify family life, since Jesus had made the father-child relationship the cornerstone of the gospel, and he saw marriage as the place where such association finds its ideal possibilities. Ideal marriage must rest not on fluctuating sentiment or the fickleness of sex attraction but on genuine mutual devotion. When such small units are gathered together, a civilization of maturity becomes possible. For people today worn down by isolation, the insight that deep friendship and a faithful home are the soil of spiritual growth is a practical one.
p160.s3.h: III. The Lures of Maturity — Worship as the Source of Energy
p160.s3.b0: Maturity requires work, and work requires energy. Rodan stated flatly that this energy does not come from emotional excitement, which instead exhausts both mind and body. Pointing to Jesus, who was even then out in the hills taking in power, he said the secret lies in spiritual communion—in worship.
p160.s3.b2: Meditation brings the mind into contact with spirit, and relaxation determines the capacity for spiritual receptivity. As these experiences are repeated they become habits of worship; habits form spiritual character, and character becomes a mature personality. His remark that such practices are difficult and time-consuming at first but become restful and timesaving once they are habits is a realistic encouragement for anyone beginning a life of prayer and meditation.
p160.s3.b3: Rodan believed there are times when one must fight for what is right, but he said the Master would gain the same victory gracefully through tact and tolerance. All too often, when we battle for the right, both victor and vanquished suffer defeat. His observation that we often enter a fight merely to convince ourselves that we are not afraid is a sharp one.
p160.s3.b5: Rodan said the gospel supplies a new and richer incentive for higher living. The very concept of an eternal and divine goal calls forth the best in man and lifts him above lower irritations such as worry, jealousy, and revenge. But he cautioned that the life purpose must be guarded from the temptation of easy and transient attainment and made immune to the threats of fanaticism.
p160.s4.h: IV. The Balance of Maturity — Making a Living and the Art of Defeat
p160.s4.b0: The spirit is our goal, but the flesh is a fact. Rodan named the two major problems of life as making a temporal living and achieving eternal survival, and said that even making a living requires religion for its ideal solution. He listed six essentials of temporal life.

head: Essentials of temporal life
Rodan’s emphasis
rows: Good physical health
Body and mind are the dwelling place of the gift of the Gods
Clear and clean thinking
The mind mediates between material things and spiritual realities
Ability and skill
Ability is inherited, skill acquired; skill is a source of satisfaction
Wealth — the goods of life
Industry alone is not enough; wise planning and organized channels are needed
Ability to withstand defeat
Learn to lose cheerfully; never hide failure
Culture — education and wisdom
Wisdom dominates knowledge and glorifies culture

p160.s4.b2: Rodan urged his hearers to treasure in memory the strength-giving episodes of life and so build up reserve galleries of beauty and goodness. The noblest of these memories are the recollections of the great moments of a superb friendship.
p160.s4.b3: He laid special stress on the art of defeat. Always claiming success and hiding failure behind smiles creates a world of unreality that ends in the crash of disillusionment. Wisdom comes only from the experience of adjusting to the results of one’s failures.
p160.s4.b5: Because wisdom embraces both fact and ideal, it saves us from two barren extremes: idealism that excludes facts and materialism without spiritual outlook. Rodan also called skill a real source of satisfaction in living, and advised that even as pleasure seekers we should be producers as well as consumers.
p160.s4.b7: A life whose whole temporal enterprise appears a failure may prove a great success in the light of eternity, provided each failure yielded wisdom and spirit achievement. This attitude—neither denying failure nor being crushed by it—offers deep freedom in an age that measures people by results.
p160.s5.h: V. The Religion of the Ideal — The Word God and the Reality of God
p160.s5.b0: For Rodan, religion is the experience of reacting to something one regards as worthy of the devotion of all mankind. So when something has truly become one’s religion, one has already become its evangel. He called religions based on fear, emotion, tradition, and philosophy intellectual religions, and those based on true spirit experience true religions.

head: Point of contrast
Lower religion
Higher religion
rows: Basis
Fear, emotion, tradition, philosophy
True spirit experience
God
The word God, the idea of God
The ideal of God, the reality of the eternal God
Direction
Shapes the idea of God to suit the natural state of the human heart
Demands that the human heart be changed to meet the ideals of true religion
Result
A religion of wishful imagination
Living spiritual experience and real spirit progression

p160.s5.b2: Rodan held that Jesus’ religion transcends all earlier ideas of worship, because Jesus not only portrayed the Father as the ideal of infinite reality but declared that he is personally attainable by every mortal who enters the kingdom. Rodan confessed that he himself had now set out as a believer.
p160.s5.b4: Rodan did not hide the cost. To enter the kingdom one must be born again and be willing to undergo the terrible and testing process of self-destruction and soul reconstruction. Only after paying the price of dedication to the Father’s will do we experience great peace on the path of consecrated living. Read alongside his statement that true religion seeks to convert the individual and transform the world, this shows that faith is a call to change before it is a comfort.
p160.s5.b6: Finally Rodan said that the impulse to be like God, the emotion of worship, the conviction to serve God, and the reasoning that this religion is best are not, in themselves, true religion. All of these must be made personal by the revelation of the Spirit of Truth. It is a call not to leave religion at the level of thought or feeling but to make it living experience.
p160.s6.b0: Paper 160 records how one thoughtful man absorbed the gospel into a philosophy of living. Rodan confessed that his philosophy had given him the urge to search but no driving power or direction, and that Jesus’ gospel supplied the insight, ideals, and settled goals he lacked. He shows that philosophy and faith need not exclude each other but can complete each other.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Name your problems honestly instead of avoiding them
Only a brave person faces them (160:1.7)
Make withdrawing alone to worship a habit
Worshipful meditation (160:1.10, 160:3.2)
Cultivate deep friendship and a faithful home
Four factors of the art of living (160:2.6)
Look for the key rather than breaking down the door
Tact and tolerance (160:3.4)
Do not hide failure; turn it into wisdom
The art of defeat (160:4.13, 160:4.15)
Worship the reality of God, not merely the word
The religion of the ideal (160:5.6)

p160.s6.b2: In the next paper, Paper 161, “Further Discussions with Rodan,” Rodan, Nathaniel, and Thomas discuss more deeply the personality of God and the divine nature of Jesus.
p161.lead: Nathaniel and Thomas continue their debate with Rodan: Is God a person? Is Jesus divine? And how did the human and divine minds work together in Jesus?

p161.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p161.s0.h: Introduction — Two Apostles Stay Behind at Magadan
p161.s0.b0: On September 25, A.D. 29, Jesus surprised everyone by announcing that early the next morning he and the twelve would set out for Jerusalem to attend the feast of tabernacles. The evangelists were told to visit the believers in Galilee, and the women’s corps to return for a while to Bethsaida.
p161.s0.b1: Nathaniel and Thomas, however, had not finished their discussions with Rodan, and with the Master’s permission they stayed on at Magadan for a few more days. During the previous week the two had taken turns presenting the gospel to the Greek philosopher, and Rodan found that what he had learned at Alexandria from a former apostle of John the Baptist fitted well with Jesus’ teachings. This paper records the conversation about the two questions that remained: the personality of God and the divinity of Jesus.
p161.s1.h: I. The Personality of God — A Philosopher’s Objection and Nathaniel’s Argument
p161.s1.b0: Rodan readily accepted everything presented to him about the attributes of God, but he insisted that God cannot be a person as man conceives personality. The text adds a nice touch of wit: the apostles found it hard to prove that God is a person, but Rodan found it still harder to prove that he is not.
p161.s1.b1: Rodan’s reasoning ran like this. Personality consists in full and mutual communication between beings of equality. But the infinite and eternal Creator has no equals, so God may be the source of personality while himself standing beyond it.
p161.s1.b3: The two apostles asked Jesus to come to their rescue, but he declined to enter the discussion. He only told Thomas that there was something more important than the idea itself.
p161.s1.b5: Thomas argued that God communicates with man and is therefore a person, and Nathaniel appealed to his own experience of God. Rodan granted that he had recently had similar experiences, but he maintained that experience proves only the reality of God, not his personality. By Monday night Thomas gave up; but by Tuesday night Nathaniel had changed Rodan’s mind through five steps of reasoning.
p161.s1.b6: It was a philosopher’s rigor that led Rodan to accept the reality of the experience while questioning the personality behind it. To have experienced God is one thing; to explain who God is is another. The distinction is a good example for anyone who treasures religious experience yet does not want to turn it hastily into doctrine.

head: Step
Nathaniel’s argument
rows: 1. The Trinity
The Father enjoys equality of communication with the Eternal Son and the Infinite Spirit, who are fully equal to him
2. Jesus’ manifestation
The Son, equal with the Father, revealed personality to his earth children — settling whether God and man can communicate
3. The mediator of communication
Jesus kept understanding communication with both God and man — two things related to the same thing are related to each other
4. The highest concept
Personality is man’s highest concept of human reality, God his highest concept of divine reality — God is an infinite personality
5. Origin and destiny
As Creator and destiny of all personality, God must be a personality

p161.s1.b8: In the first argument, once Rodan considered the doctrine of the Trinity, he had to concede that the Universal Father might be a person. The text adds that later reflection on these discussions gave the twelve apostles an enlarged conception of the Trinity. A debate meant to persuade a philosopher ended by widening the apostles’ own understanding. That teaching becomes learning is something faith communities still discover today.
p161.s1.b9: The heart of the third argument is that Jesus stands in the middle. He was one with the Father and at the same time in perfect communication with men. Since both God and man understood the symbols of his communication, both must possess the attributes of personality. The argument that Jesus’ personality demonstrates God’s personality while proving the presence of God in man puts into philosophical language the truth that knowing Jesus is the way to know God.
p161.s1.b10: On the fifth argument, the text tells us that Rodan had been tremendously influenced by Jesus’ teaching, “⟦Q 161:1.10⟧Be you therefore perfect, even as your Father in heaven is perfect.⟦/Q⟧” If the Creator and destiny of personality were not himself a person, the call for personal beings to become perfect like him would lose its meaning. Because the goal toward which we move is a Person, the path of growth becomes a path of relationship.
p161.s1.b12: Rodan’s conclusion is a model of honest intellect reconciled with faith. He confessed God as a person, qualifying the word with such values as transcendent, infinite, and universal, and he accepted Jesus as the personal revelation of the Father and the satisfaction of everything left unsatisfied in philosophy. To believe that God is personal is not to pull him down to the human level; it is to be assured that we can have a true relationship with him.
p161.s2.h: II. The Divine Nature of Jesus — The Witness of Those Who Lived with Him
p161.s2.b0: The last question was the teaching about Jesus’ divine nature, which had only recently been announced publicly. Nathaniel and Thomas presented their views together, and the text gives them in nine condensed and rearranged points. The strength of this testimony lies not in abstract argument but in years of watching a life at close range.

head: Point
Jesus as the two apostles saw him
rows: 1. His own admission
He admitted his divinity, and some events can be understood only by believing it
2. Friendship
The most unselfish friend, who reproves yet truly loves — only a divine being could be such a friend
3. A blameless life
He makes no mistakes and has nothing to repent of; he prays for us but never asks us to pray for him
4. A unique character
Perfect emotional control and compassion that answers every kind of suffering
5. One who knows hearts
He understands men’s thoughts and longings; he prays like a man but performs like a God
6. Superhuman knowledge
He asks questions to draw us out, not to gain information
7. Authority
He speaks with the authority of a divine teacher; brave yet free from pride
8. Partnership with God
“Before Abraham was, I am”; he speaks of being one with the Father with childlike naturalness
9. His prayer life
He prays as if talking with God face to face

p161.s2.b3: It is worth noticing that friendship came first among the apostles’ reasons. They said Jesus was the friend even of sinners, that he dared to love his enemies, and that while he did not hesitate to reprove them, he truly loved them. Through all the years they failed to grasp his mission, he remained a faithful friend. That the first evidence of his divinity was not a miracle but a friendship tells us that the surest way God is revealed is through a relationship of love.
p161.s2.b4: They said too that his compassion was moved alike by physical suffering, mental anguish, and spiritual sorrow, and that he was quick to recognize and generous to acknowledge faith and every other grace in others. He did not crave the support of the multitude, was indifferent to the opinions of men, and was brave yet free from pride. The picture of him speaking the most astounding claims with childlike naturalness shows that true authority appears not in display but in naturalness.
p161.s2.b6: This short sentence sums up the whole of the two apostles’ witness. He seemed to know men’s thoughts and understand their longings; he possessed all human emotions, but magnificently glorified. He loved goodness strongly and hated sin equally; he was kind yet brave, and never faltered in doing his duty. Here the human and the divine are blended in one personality without conflict.
p161.s2.b8: The two apostles said that Jesus was either what he professed to be or else the greatest hypocrite and fraud the world had ever known, and they were persuaded of the former. They knew he was human, and they were almost equally sure that he was also divine.
p161.s2.b10: When their talks were over, the two reached Jerusalem on Friday, and the other apostles learned much from their account of the experience. Rodan returned to Alexandria, where he long taught in the school of Meganta, and he gave up his life in Greece when the persecutions were at their height. One week of earnest discussion changed a philosopher’s whole life.
p161.s3.h: III. Jesus’ Human and Divine Minds — The Narrator’s Confession
p161.s3.b0: In the final section the narrator speaks directly. Jesus’ consciousness of divinity grew gradually until his baptism; after that he seems to have had the power to limit, in various ways, his human consciousness of his divinity. It appears that he could freely choose whether to depend only on the human mind or to use the knowledge of both the human and the divine minds.

head: Mode the narrator observed
What it looked like
rows: Self-limiting divine consciousness
At times he used only the information resident in the human intellect
Concealing foreknowledge and thought discernment
He foreknew events and read thoughts but kept his associates from knowing this too fully
The divine mind at work
He conferred with the directors of the celestial hosts
The combined personality at work
Acts activated by the perfect union of the human and divine minds — witnessed on almost numberless occasions

p161.s3.b2: Jesus held back his powers because he did not wish to go too far beyond the concept of the human held in his apostles’ minds. It was a kind of consideration that shows others only as much as they can bear. The narrator candidly admits that he could not always tell the two methods apart.
p161.s3.b3: This section fits with the apostles’ testimony before it. The superhuman knowledge and foreknowledge they saw were the working of the divine mind; his praying like a man was the working of the human mind. Jesus lived as a combined personality that cannot be reduced to either one. That he often chose to act with the human mind alone shows that his life on earth was truly a human life.
p161.s3.b5: When even a superhuman narrator confesses that he does not know, we are taught humility before mystery. To reason faithfully as far as we can, and then leave what lies beyond as mystery, is a virtue needed both in Rodan’s philosophy and in the apostles’ faith.
p161.s4.b0: Paper 161 is a conversation in which faith and reason meet head on. Rodan objected with logic, Nathaniel answered with logic, and the two apostles bore witness from a life lived together. And Jesus reminded them that spiritual acquaintance with the Father’s nature matters more than any idea about him.

p161.s4.b2: In the next paper, Paper 162, “At the Feast of Tabernacles,” Jesus goes up to Jerusalem despite his apostles’ fears and teaches openly in the temple courts.
p162.lead: “My hour has come”: Jesus teaches openly in Jerusalem at great risk — the woman taken in adultery, the light of the world, the water of life, and the freedom of the soul.

p162.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p162.s0.h: Introduction — Turned Away by a Samaritan Village
p162.s0.b0: Jesus and the ten apostles meant to travel to Jerusalem by way of Samaria. But a village on the slopes of Mount Gilboa refused them lodging because Jesus was a Jew, and drove off Philip and Matthew, who had shown their anger, with sticks and stones. James and John then asked permission to bid fire come down from heaven to devour the villagers.
p162.s0.b2: Jesus did not argue; he simply turned toward another little village by the Jordan ford. The narrator notes that because of sectarian prejudice those Samaritans denied themselves the honor of showing hospitality to the Creator Son of a universe. The response to insult was not revenge but a change of road, and in that sense this brief episode sets the tone for the whole paper.
p162.s1.h: I. The Dangers of the Visit to Jerusalem — Protected by Boldness
p162.s1.b0: His followers had long urged Jesus to proclaim the gospel in Jerusalem, but now that he meant to go, they feared for his life. They knew the Sanhedrin intended to bring him to trial, and he had repeatedly told them he must meet death. Where he had once said, “My hour has not yet come,” he now answered only that his hour had come.
p162.s1.b1: Several reasons combined to allow him to teach openly in the temple courts and still leave alive. The text’s explanation can be summed up as follows.

head: Reason
The text’s explanation
rows: A divided Sanhedrin
Many members were secret believers or firmly opposed to an arrest during the feast
A friendly crowd
Many of the assembled pilgrims believed in Jesus or were well disposed toward his spiritual movement
The work of Abner’s group
They had built up sentiment favorable to the kingdom throughout Judea
Boldness itself
His unexpected public appearance overawed his enemies and caught them unprepared
A mistaken guess
His enemies supposed the Roman authorities or Philip had promised him protection

p162.s1.b3: Those who heard him were divided. Some called him a good man, a prophet, the true Messiah; others denounced him as a mischief-maker leading the people astray. His enemies feared to denounce him openly because of the believing crowd, and his friends feared to acknowledge him openly because of the leaders. Yet even his enemies, who knew he had never studied in the rabbinical schools, marveled at his teaching.
p162.s1.b4: His mere appearance in Jerusalem at the feast of tabernacles put an end forever to the rumor that he had fled to Phoenicia out of fear. The text says that this teaching in Solomon’s Porch and the temple courts was in effect the formal announcement of Jesus’ divinity to the Jewish people and the world. As the apostles heard him speak more boldly day by day, their fears only grew.
p162.s2.h: II. The First Temple Talk — Eber Returns Empty-Handed
p162.s2.b0: Asked how he could teach so fluently when he had never studied under the rabbis, Jesus answered that his teaching was not his own but belonged to the One who sent him. And he placed the test of it not in knowledge but in the will.
p162.s2.b2: He explained that the rulers sought to kill him because of a gospel that frees people from formal, ceremonial religion and heavy tradition, and he appealed to them to judge not by appearances but by the true spirit of his teaching. Then he spoke without malice to Eber, the Sanhedrin officer sent to arrest him, inviting him not to be afraid to come closer.
p162.s2.b4: Eber came back without Jesus and reported that he had never heard a man speak like this man. When the leaders rebuked him, he asked in turn whether the law did not require fairness, and whether they would condemn a man before hearing him. A man who went out to do his duty listened to the teaching and ended by following the voice of his conscience.
p162.s3.h: III. The Woman Taken in Adultery — A Distorted Record and What Really Happened
p162.s3.b0: The text states that the record of this episode as it has come down to us is distorted. Jesus knew the scribes and Pharisees were blinded by tradition, but he also knew they were among the most thoroughly moral men of their day. In fact, it was agents hired by the Sanhedrin who brought the woman before him.

head: Jesus’ choice
The trap his enemies had prepared
rows: If he said, “Stone her”
A death sentence without approval of the Roman courts would bring him into conflict with the Roman rulers
If he said, “Do not stone her”
They would accuse him before the Sanhedrin of setting himself above Moses and the Jewish law
If he kept silent
They would accuse him of cowardice

p162.s3.b2: The woman was the wife of a man who had been a troublemaker in Nazareth in Jesus’ youth; her husband had made her a source of income and had handed her over in a deal with the rulers’ hirelings. Jesus went to where the husband stood behind the crowd and wrote in the sand, and the husband was the first to leave. Then the accusers, and finally the woman’s companion in evil, read what he wrote and went away one by one.
p162.s3.b4: The woman’s name was Hildana; she left her wicked husband and joined the disciples of the kingdom. Jesus did not publicly shame the plotters, yet he let the trap collapse under its own weight. The scene shows that justice and mercy need not stand opposed; they can stand together.
p162.s4.h: IV. The Feast of Tabernacles — The Feast of Feasts
p162.s4.b0: The feast of tabernacles, which drew people from all over the known world, from Spain to India, was an ideal occasion for Jesus to proclaim his full gospel publicly. The cool autumn weather brought more Jews than either Passover or Pentecost, and sacrifices missed at other feasts could all be offered at this one.

head: Feature of the feast
Meaning and appearance
rows: Seventy bullocks
A symbol of the seventy nations of the heathen world
The water ceremony
A symbol of the outpouring of the divine spirit
Great candlesticks and torches

Three groups on the final morning
One attending the morning sacrifice, one cutting willow branches, one in procession to draw water from Siloam
Wine and water poured on the altar
The signal to begin singing the psalms and waving the branches

p162.s4.b2: Only the Roman tower of Antonia looked down on the brilliant festivities in grim contrast. Jesus’ two discourses that followed take hold of these very symbols of light and water and point to the spiritual realities behind them.
p162.s5.h: V–VI. Sermon on the Light of the World; Discourse on the Water of Life
p162.s5.b1: On the evening before the last day, while the candlesticks and torches lit the scene, Jesus stood up and declared that he was the light of the world. He said he knew where he came from, who he was, and where he was going, and that his hearers judged only by the appearances of the flesh and did not perceive the realities of the spirit. He judged no one, he said, and if he did judge, he would judge together with the Father.
p162.s5.b3: He foretold that when the Son of Man was lifted up, all would know who he was. He did nothing of himself but did as the Father had taught him, and because he did what was pleasing in the Father’s sight, he was not alone. Many who heard believed, and no one dared to lay hands on him.
p162.s5.b4: On the great day of the feast, just after the priests had poured the water and wine on the altar, Jesus called out that whoever was thirsty should come to him and drink. He did not interrupt the ceremony; he spoke in the brief interval while the Hallel was finished and the offerings prepared. What he promised was the Spirit of Truth, to be poured out on all flesh when his work on earth was done.
p162.s5.b6: Jesus granted that their fathers had done well to symbolize the outpouring of the spirit, yet he asked why they would water their souls with the traditions of men, poured from the broken pitchers of ceremonial service. The point of the discourse is to honor the symbol but press on to the reality it points to.
p162.s6.h: VII. The Discourse on Spiritual Freedom — Before Abraham Was
p162.s6.b0: On the afternoon of the last day, Jesus told the believers in Solomon’s Porch that the truth would make them free. The freedom he meant was not outward release from another’s rule but the liberty of the soul.

p162.s6.b3: He said that it is the Father who would glorify him, and that he had come to show people how to become truly sons of God. When an uproar broke out, he said only, “⟦Q 162:7.6⟧Before Abraham was, I am⟦/Q⟧,” and slipped away to a secret meeting place near Bethany, where Martha, Mary, and Lazarus were waiting for him.
p162.s7.h: VIII–IX. The Visit with Martha and Mary; At Bethlehem with Abner
p162.s7.b0: In the home of his friends at Bethany, Mary sat at Jesus’ feet listening to his teaching while Martha busied herself preparing the evening meal. The text explains that Martha was given to being needlessly distracted by many unnecessary tasks. Jesus’ answer did not merely take Mary’s side; it called both sisters to co-operation.
p162.s7.b2: During the feast Jesus divided his time almost equally between Bethany and Bethlehem. At Bethlehem he taught Abner and the former apostles of John the Baptist, who, moved by the courage they had seen in Jerusalem and the sympathy they experienced in his personal teaching, wholeheartedly accepted the kingdom. Early in November, Abner and his eleven associates joined Jesus and the twelve in a single organization.
p162.s8.b0: Paper 162 shows Jesus speaking most boldly in the very midst of danger. Yet his boldness was not aggression. He took no revenge on the village that insulted him, bore no ill will toward the officer sent to arrest him, and did not condemn the woman used as bait in a trap. The courage to proclaim truth and the mercy with which he treated people lived together in one man.

Vengeance is not the outlook of the kingdom (162:0.2)

p162.s8.b2: In the next paper, Paper 163, “Ordination of the Seventy at Magadan,” Jesus commissions new messengers and prepares for the final stage of the kingdom’s work.
p163.lead: Magadan, where seventy gospel messengers were ordained and sent out: the rich young man Matadormus, the teaching on wealth, and the final phase that began at Pella.

p163.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p163.s0.b0: A few days after the return from Jerusalem, Abner came from Bethlehem to Magadan with about fifty of his disciples. Gathered at the camp were the evangelistic corps, the women’s corps, and about one hundred and fifty tried disciples from all parts of Palestine. Jesus opened an intensive course of training for them, intending to choose seventy teachers from among them and send them out.
p163.s0.b1: The training ran from Friday, November 4, to the Sabbath, November 19. Jesus lectured every morning, and the apostles divided the work according to their experience and gifts.

p163.s1.h: I. Ordination of the Seventy — Lambs Among Wolves
p163.s1.b0: On the Sabbath afternoon of November 19, amid passing showers, more than four hundred believers watched the ordination by the shore of the Sea of Galilee. The seventy were made up of ten of Abner’s fellow apostles of John, fifty-one of the earlier evangelists, and eight other disciples who had distinguished themselves in the service of the kingdom; Abner was made their chief.
p163.s1.b1: Before laying his hands on them, Jesus told them how they were to go. They were to go two and two, without purse or extra clothing, stay in a home where peace-loving people lived, and not move from house to house for the sake of better lodging.
p163.s1.b3: Even when leaving a city that rejected the gospel, they were not to withdraw their message. People may refuse the truth, but the fact that the kingdom of God has come near remains. The next morning Abner sent the thirty-five pairs out to the cities of Galilee, Samaria, and Judea; they taught for about six weeks and returned on December 30 to the new camp near Pella.
p163.s2.h: II. The Rich Young Man and Others — Undivided Affections
p163.s2.b0: More than fifty disciples who sought ordination as members of the seventy were rejected by a committee made up of Andrew, Abner, and the acting head of the evangelistic corps. Candidates on whom the committee disagreed were brought to Jesus, and he never directly turned anyone away. But more than a dozen, after talking with him, withdrew of their own accord.
p163.s2.b1: To a disciple who wished first to go and bury his father, Jesus said he could return home to care for his loved ones and still remain a loyal disciple. But the messengers of the gospel, he said, were those who had forsaken all. The distinction matters: Jesus clearly separated being a disciple from being an ordained messenger.
p163.s2.b2: The rich young man Matadormus, a member of the Sanhedrin, said he had kept the commandments from his youth and asked about eternal life. Jesus answered that since he believed the gospel, he was already a disciple and a child of the kingdom. But Matadormus was not content to be a disciple; he wanted to be a messenger, and Jesus told him to sell his goods, give them away, and follow him.
p163.s2.b4: He went away sorrowful. The text explains that what Jesus wanted was to deliver him not from his wealth as such but from the love of wealth. Had he given up his property, it would probably have been put right back into his hands as treasurer of the seventy. Years later he did obey the Master’s injunction, but by then it was too late to be one of the seventy.

head: Jesus’ attitude toward wealth
The text’s explanation
rows: Possession itself
He never taught that it was wrong to have wealth
The demand to give up everything
Applied only to the twelve and the seventy, and even then he took care that goods be disposed of to advantage
Surplus income
Wise investment was a legitimate form of insurance against future adversity
Economic abuses he condemned
The unfair exploitation of the weak and untaught by the strong and shrewd
The real test
Not wealth but the love of wealth — servility to mammon

p163.s2.b8: The text also draws attention to freedom of choice in this episode. The forces of the spiritual world do not coerce a person; they allow him to go the way he has chosen. The decision always remains a person’s own.
p163.s3.h: III. The Discussion about Wealth — The Parable of the Vineyard Laborers
p163.s3.b0: After the young man left, Jesus said how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the spiritual life. When the astonished Peter asked who then could be saved, he answered that not all who have wealth are excluded, and that with God all things are possible. He grieved that Matadormus had not stayed, for he greatly loved him.
p163.s3.b2: To Peter’s question about what those who had left everything would receive, Jesus answered that they would receive many times as much in this world and eternal life in the world to come, adding that the first may be last. Then he told the parable of laborers hired at different hours of the day who all receive a denarius. The point of the parable is that the Father deals with his creatures according to their needs and in accordance with his just laws of merciful consideration.
p163.s4.h: IV. Farewell to the Seventy — Seven Charges and Six Virtues
p163.s4.b0: On the morning the seventy departed, Jesus emphasized seven points in his farewell talk. Then Peter took them aside and preached a sermon expounding the Master’s ordination charge, urging six virtues upon them.

head: No.
Jesus’ charge
rows: Proclaim the gospel to Jew and gentile alike, to the whole world
In ministering to the sick, refrain from teaching them to expect miracles
Proclaim a spiritual brotherhood of the sons of God, not an outward kingdom
Do not waste time in excessive social visiting and trivialities
If the first home is worthy, stay there for the whole time in that city
Make it known that the time has come for an open break with the religious leaders at Jerusalem
Teach that the whole duty of man is summed up in one commandment: love God and love your neighbor

head: Virtue Peter urged
What it meant
rows: Consecrated devotion
Praying for laborers leads one to say, “Here am I; send me”; daily worship
Real courage

Faith and trust

p163.s4.b3: The text puts no symbolism on the number seventy. The Jews did regard seventy as a significant number, but it was an accident that this group numbered exactly seventy. Jesus would have accepted at least six more, but they were unwilling to pay the price of giving up wealth and family.
p163.s5.h: V–VI. Moving the Camp to Pella; The Return of the Seventy
p163.s5.b0: On December 6 a company of nearly three hundred moved to Pella, near the place where Jesus had been baptized, by the spring where John the Baptist had once camped. David Zebedee, on his own initiative, brought the camp equipment from Bethsaida and prepared to receive nearly fifteen hundred people, for even in the rainy season earnest seekers came from all over Palestine and the Roman world.
p163.s5.b1: When the seventy returned on December 30, their reports delayed the evening meal by more than an hour. Jesus saw that people would go out proclaiming the good news without his presence, and he knew his departure would not greatly hinder the progress of the kingdom. He told them to rejoice in something other than the subjection of minor spirits.
p163.s5.b3: Just before the evening meal Jesus, in one of those rare moments of emotional ecstasy, gave thanks to the Father that this gospel had been hidden from the wise and self-righteous but revealed to the children of the kingdom, and that the good news would spread through all the world after his departure. He said that when he had finished his revelation to his brethren in the flesh, he would continue it to the creatures on high. Then he turned to his disciples and reminded them of the privilege they enjoyed.
p163.s5.b5: He called blessed the communities that had received the gospel, yet lamented over Chorazin, Bethsaida-Julias, and Capernaum, which had not received the messengers well. The more light a place has received, the heavier its responsibility for rejecting that light.
p163.s5.b6: The next day he solemnly warned the seventy against the subtlety of spiritual pride: if they understood the fall of Lucifer, they would shun every form of spiritual pride. He told them not to grow weary in well doing and repeated his invitation to all who labor and are heavy laden.
p163.s6.h: VII. Preparation for the Last Mission — The Phase of Spiritual Depth
p163.s6.b0: The Pella camp prepared for a final three-month tour throughout Perea. Jesus no longer needed to go far afield; people came to him from Palestine, the Roman world, and the Near East. The twelve women trained a new women’s corps of fifty, and Perpetua, Peter’s wife, took charge of the enlarged women’s ministry.
p163.s6.b1: The text calls this the phase of spiritual depth, in contrast to the wonder-seeking crowds of the Galilean days. Even so, not a few still failed to grasp the truth that the kingdom of heaven is the spiritual brotherhood of man founded on the universal fatherhood of God.
p163.s7.b0: Paper 163 marks the turning point at which the kingdom’s work passes from Jesus alone to many trained hands. At its center is a clear distinction between levels of calling. Anyone becomes a child of the kingdom by faith, but special service carries the price of undivided affections. And whether to pay that price is always a person’s own decision.

The teaching behind it

Do not envy the portion others receive
The parable of the vineyard laborers (163:3.7)
When rejected, still offer the truth calmly
The kingdom has still come near (163:1.4)

Be not lifted up (163:6.2)

p163.s7.b2: In the next paper, Paper 164, “At the Feast of Dedication,” Jesus goes up to Jerusalem again and faces a storm of controversy after healing a man blind from birth.
p164.lead: One more chance for the Sanhedrin to see the light: the story of the good Samaritan, the gathering at Nicodemus’s house, and the healing of the blind beggar Josiah and his brave testimony.

p164.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p164.s0.b0: While the camp at Pella was being set up, Jesus went up secretly to the feast of dedication, taking only Nathaniel and Thomas with him. Not until they had crossed the Jordan did the two apostles realize where he was going, and they used every argument to dissuade him, pointing to the folly and danger of placing himself in the hands of the Sanhedrin. His reply never changed.
p164.s0.b2: If the visit at the feast of tabernacles had been for pilgrims from all over the empire, this visit had a single purpose: to give the Sanhedrin and the Jewish leaders another chance to see the light. Though he expected most of them would not accept the gospel, he gave every one of them one more opportunity to choose. This paper shows a love that does not close the door even on those it expects to refuse.
p164.s1.h: I. Story of the Good Samaritan — Who Proved to Be the Neighbor?
p164.s1.b0: One evening while they were staying at Jericho, a lawyer asked how to inherit eternal life. Jesus had him state the law’s two commandments of love himself, and answered that if he truly did these things, he would attain eternal life. Then the lawyer asked who his neighbor was. It was a trap meant to draw from Jesus a statement contrary to Jewish law, which limited one’s neighbor to one’s own people.
p164.s1.b1: Instead of falling into the trap, Jesus told a story any Jericho audience would fully appreciate. A priest and a Levite passed by a man left half dead by robbers, while a Samaritan bound up his wounds, brought him to an inn, and even paid for his care.

head: Who came by
What he did
Meaning in the story
rows: The priest
Saw his plight and passed by on the other side of the road
A religious office does not make one a neighbor
The Levite
Saw the man and passed by on the other side
Knowing the law is not the same as mercy
The Samaritan
Moved with compassion, bound up his wounds and cared for him at the inn
The despised one proved to be the true neighbor

p164.s1.b3: The lawyer, unwilling even to say the word “Samaritan,” answered, “⟦Q 164:1.3⟧He who showed mercy on him.⟦/Q⟧” So he himself gave the answer that, spoken by Jesus, would have furnished grounds for a charge of heresy. The text judges the story a beautiful admonition to Jesus’ followers and a stunning rebuke to the Jews for their attitude toward the Samaritans.
p164.s1.b5: This short story moved the definition of neighbor from the boundaries of blood and religion to the realm of deeds. The text adds that ever since, it has fostered brotherly love among all who have believed Jesus’ gospel. While the questioner was weighing who qualified as a neighbor, the story asked the listener to become one.
p164.s2.h: II. At Jerusalem — The Gathering at Nicodemus’s House
p164.s2.b0: The chief event of this visit took place on Friday night at the home of Nicodemus. About twenty-five Jewish leaders who believed in Jesus gathered there, fourteen of them present or recent members of the Sanhedrin. Eber, Matadormus, and Joseph of Arimathea were among them.
p164.s2.b1: Before this learned audience Jesus displayed, for the first time since his teaching in Alexandria and Rome, his broad learning and insight into human affairs. They proposed ways to win over the rest of the Sanhedrin, but Jesus only listened in silence. To the suggestion that they stand together before the seventy, he replied that this would only bring wrath on their heads, and told them each to work as the spirit led.
p164.s2.b2: When the meeting ended, all present sensed something mysterious in the Master’s personality, were charmed by his gracious manner, and came to love him. Yet as Jesus went to the Mount of Olives for the night, he had not yet decided how to bring his work once more to the Sanhedrin’s attention. The way came the next morning, near the temple, in an unexpected form.
p164.s3.h: III. Healing the Blind Beggar — Not Because of Sin
p164.s3.b0: On the Sabbath morning near the temple, Jesus saw Josiah, a beggar blind from birth, and at that moment the way to bring his mission once more before the leaders came to him. Nathaniel asked whose sin had caused this man’s blindness. At the time, many notions were current that saw a birth defect as the result of sin.

head: Belief of the time
The text’s explanation
rows: The father’s sin
A child might be born blind as punishment for some particular sin of the father
Sin before birth
A child might itself sin before it came into the world
The mother’s sin
Defects might result from the mother’s sin or indulgence while carrying the child
Reincarnation
The theory that one reaps in this life what was sown in a former one
A contradictory practice
Though blindness was thought a result of sin, giving alms to the blind was considered noble

p164.s3.b3: Jesus made clear that the blindness had come about in the natural course of events. He repeatedly warned his apostles to seek the true causes of all phenomena and to avoid the tendency to attach spiritual causes to ordinary physical events. This refusal to brand a suffering person with the stigma of sin is an important correction for today’s reader as well.
p164.s3.b4: He made clay with spittle, put it on Josiah’s eyes, and told him to wash in the pool of Siloam. Josiah had not asked to be healed and his faith was feeble, but having overheard the conversation and taking this man to be a great teacher or prophet, he did as he was told. The text gives three reasons for this use of material means.

head: Reason
Explanation
rows: First
It was not a response to individual faith but a deed of Jesus’ own choosing, arranged so the man would receive lasting benefit
Second
To encourage a man who had not asked and whose faith was weak — the ceremony held just enough to prompt him to act
Third
To teach his followers not to despise or neglect material means in healing the sick, nor to regard miracles as the only method of cure

p164.s3.b7: Having always been a beggar, Josiah went back to his usual place of alms-seeking once the first excitement of his new sight had passed. When neighbors whispered whether this was really the beggar, he answered that he was, but he did not know where the man who healed him was. He did not yet know the meaning of much that he saw. He had received grace but did not yet understand what it meant.
p164.s3.b9: The chief purpose of this deed was an open challenge to the Sanhedrin and the religious leaders, a public declaration of the break with the Pharisees. So in the afternoon Jesus sent the two apostles to Josiah to stir up a controversy deliberately, so that the Pharisees could not fail to take notice of the miracle.
p164.s4.h: IV. Josiah Before the Sanhedrin — A Growing Testimony
p164.s4.b0: The Sanhedrin convened its council in violation of its own rule against meeting on the Sabbath. Jesus had hoped to stand before them over a Sabbath healing in order to expose this very point, but they were afraid to summon him and called only Josiah. The meeting soon fell into division. To the claim that one who does not keep the Sabbath cannot be from God, younger members who secretly believed responded with pointed questions.
p164.s4.b1: His parents, when summoned, feared excommunication; they admitted only that their son had been born blind and told the council to ask him, since he was of age. Excommunication meant losing every right in Jewish society except that of buying the necessities of life. Called back again, Josiah would not bow to pressure to declare Jesus a sinner.
p164.s4.b3: When the same questions were repeated, Josiah asked whether they too wanted to become his disciples, and at last, standing on a stool, he cried out that if this man were not from God, he could not have done this. The leaders cast him out of the synagogue. The text says that most of his wise and courageous testimony grew up in his mind while the unfair trial went on.

p164.s5.h: V. Teaching in Solomon’s Porch — My Sheep Hear My Voice
p164.s5.b0: While the Sanhedrin met, Jesus taught a midwinter crowd for more than two hours nearby in Solomon’s Porch. He had hoped to be summoned so that he could proclaim the freedom and joy of divine sonship, but they were afraid even to call him as a witness. When challenged to say plainly whether he was the Messiah, he answered that the works he did in his Father’s name bore witness for him.
p164.s5.b2: When he said that he and the Father were one, some ran to pick up stones. He asked for which of his good works they meant to stone him, and told them that if they could not believe him, they should at least believe the works. Then he declared that as the Father dwelt in him, so he would dwell in all who believed the gospel.
p164.s5.b4: Only when Jesus heard that Josiah had been cast out of the synagogue did he go to find him and ask whether he believed in the Son of God. Josiah fell down, confessed his belief, and worshiped, and he was greatly encouraged when told to come with them to the camp at Pella. He spent the rest of his life as a preacher of the gospel of the kingdom.
p164.s6.b0: In Paper 164 Jesus gives the leaders another chance though he knows they will refuse, and he chooses a man from the lowest place in society as his means. A lawyer who tried to narrow the circle of neighbors ended up giving the wider answer himself, and a blind beggar spoke the truth more plainly before the court than the scholars did. The paper shows that faith does not arrive complete from the start; it grows as it is tested.

p165.lead: A last mission without miracles: teaching at the Pella camp, the sermon on the good shepherd, faith without fear, and words on wealth and watchfulness.

p165.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p165.s0.b0: On January 3, A.D. 30, Abner, chief of the seventy, gave his associates their final instructions before sending them out to the cities and villages of Perea. This Perean mission lasted almost three months and was the Master’s last ministry; when it was over, Jesus went straight to Jerusalem to pass through his final experiences in the flesh. The seventy worked in thirty-five cities and towns and in about fifty villages.
p165.s0.b1: The text spells out the character of this period. There were no miracles, and most of the ministry to the sick was carried out by the women’s corps, now sixty-two strong. Perea, half gentile and half Jew, was the most beautiful district in Palestine; it was more thoroughly worked than any other, and its better classes of citizens widely received the Master’s teaching.

head: Feature of the Perean mission
The text’s explanation
rows: Length
Almost three months — the Master’s final ministry
Workers
The seventy under Abner, periodically reinforced by Jesus and the twelve
Ministry to the sick
Carried out mostly by the sixty-two members of the women’s corps
Character
A last period in which the higher spiritual phases developed — no miracles were performed
Baptism
Given to all believers on Abner’s instructions, not by Jesus’ command

p165.s1.h: I. At the Pella Camp — Choosing to Finish at the Height
p165.s1.b0: By the middle of January more than twelve hundred people had gathered at Pella. Jesus usually taught the multitude at nine in the morning, the apostles taught in the afternoon, and in the evening he held question-and-answer sessions with about fifty advanced disciples. By the middle of March his morning audiences numbered more than four thousand.
p165.s1.b1: The text says that Jesus chose to finish his work on earth when interest in his message was at its height — the highest point reached in the second, miracle-free phase of his ministry. Three quarters of the crowd were seekers after truth, but Pharisees and fault-finders were mixed in among them. Once Abner and the seventy set out on their mission, they never again returned to Pella.
p165.s2.h: II. Sermon on the Good Shepherd — Both Door and Shepherd
p165.s2.b0: After the feast of dedication more than three hundred Pharisees and others followed Jesus from Jerusalem to Pella. With friends and enemies both present, he said he would speak in parables, and that each should take what found a welcome in his own heart. He pointed out that the sin of teachers who claim to see remains upon them.

p165.s2.b2: Jesus said that whoever would be an undershepherd must lead the flock to green pastures and still waters. Then he declared that he was both the door of the sheepfold and the true shepherd, that he would not flee in the face of danger, and that he would finish the service of completing his Father’s will.
p165.s2.b4: He added that he had other sheep not of this fold, and that these words did not refer to this world alone. All would come to know the voice of the one shepherd and be led into one brotherhood of the sons of God. He also said that no one could take his life from him; he had the power both to lay it down and to take it up again.
p165.s2.b6: The Pharisees declared him mad and went out into the night, but some of the Jerusalem teachers said he spoke like one having authority. The next day about half of those teachers professed belief in Jesus.
p165.s3.h: III. Sabbath Sermon at Pella — Trust and Spiritual Preparedness
p165.s3.b0: On January 28, before nearly three thousand people, Jesus preached on “⟦Q 165:3.1⟧Trust and Spiritual Preparedness.⟦/Q⟧” He warned them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, born of prejudice and nurtured in tradition, though he added that many of the Pharisees were honest of heart. And he told them not to fear those who can kill only the body.
p165.s3.b2: Not one sparrow exists without the Father’s knowledge, and to the seraphic guardians even the hairs of our heads are numbered. He warned too that the deliberate rebel who knowingly ascribes the works of God to the forces of evil will seldom seek forgiveness. And he promised that when they were brought before high authorities, the indwelling spirit would teach them what to say.
p165.s3.b5: These words show concisely how God’s invitation and man’s response fit together. The Father never compels anyone to enter the kingdom. For the one who lingers in the valley of decision, the only thing left is his or her own consent.
p165.s3.b6: When the sermon ended, many went down to the Jordan to be baptized by the apostles. The teaching to lay aside fear led at once to decision. Meanwhile Jesus continued teaching, listening to the questions of those who stayed behind.
p165.s4.h: IV. Dividing the Inheritance — Rich Toward God
p165.s4.b0: While the apostles were baptizing, a young man asked Jesus to make his brother divide an inheritance with him. Jesus asked who had made him a divider over them and then told everyone to beware of covetousness. He did not meddle even in the temporal affairs of his own apostles. Yet he used the question as an occasion for deeper teaching.
p165.s4.b2: He told the story of a rich man who tore down his barns to build bigger ones, stored up his goods, and planned to take his ease. That very night robbers killed him, plundered and burned his barns, and his heirs quarreled over what was left. He had laid up treasure on earth but was not rich toward God.
p165.s4.b3: Asked whether it was a sin to possess honest wealth, Jesus answered that honorable wealth is not a sin. But when wealth becomes a treasure that absorbs one’s interests and turns one’s affections away from spiritual pursuits, it is sin. He pointed to David Zebedee’s tent city, which was kept going by the gifts of generous people.

head: Three questions for those who have wealth
What to reflect on
rows: 1. How much wealth did you accumulate?
Has accumulating become an end in itself?
2. How did you get this wealth?
Was it gained honestly and honorably?
3. How did you use your wealth?
Was it shared in the spirit of a steward rather than of greed?

p165.s4.b6: Earlier, the young man had felt that Jesus treated him harshly, and while the others watched the baptisms he came back privately. Jesus heard him out again and told him that the synagogue court would administer the laws of inheritance fairly. His own work, he said, was to make known the heavenly inheritance, and he urged the young man not to give way to covetousness on a day when he might eat the bread of life. His parting question was brief and weighty.
p165.s4.b8: The text makes clear that Jesus neither taught nor tolerated improvidence, idleness, indifference to the needs of one’s family, or dependence on alms. He taught that material things must be subordinate to the welfare of the soul and the progress of the spiritual nature. To someone who asked about the judgment of rich and poor, he answered that the lives people live will judge them all.
p165.s5.h: V–VI. Talks to the Apostles on Wealth; Answer to Peter’s Question — The Watchful Steward
p165.s5.b0: That evening, at Andrew’s request, Jesus spoke to the apostles on the same subject, but he said his words to them must differ from his words to the multitude, since they had left everything to be ordained as ambassadors of the kingdom. Pointing to the ravens and the lilies, he told them not to be anxious about what they would eat or wear.

head: Who
What Jesus said about their support
rows: Apostles who gave their lives to the gospel

Believing disciples
They earn their own bread and contribute to the support of those who teach and heal
The multitude as a whole
Honorable wealth is no sin, but guard against wealth becoming your master

p165.s5.b3: Looking ahead to the severe testing to come, he told them to gird up the loins of their minds and keep their lamps burning, for the Son of Man would depart at an hour they did not expect and in a way they did not foresee. The twelve sat in silence for several minutes. They had heard such warnings before, but never in circumstances like these.
p165.s5.b4: When Peter asked whether this parable was meant for the apostles alone, Jesus answered that he would entrust the welfare of his children to the faithful steward who had endured trial. By contrast, the servant who thinks his master delays his coming and begins to mistreat his fellows will be cast out in disgrace.
p165.s5.b7: Jesus said honestly that his mission would not bring peace to the material affairs of men, at least not for a time. The gospel would cause division even within families. Yet each believer would have great and lasting peace in his own heart, and they were still to proclaim this gospel to all the world.
p165.s6.b0: Paper 165 opens the period in which, with miracles gone, the teaching grows deepest. As a shepherd Jesus guards the sheep, and he teaches trust instead of fear, heavenly treasure instead of possessions, and watchfulness instead of complacency. In the end these teachings come down to one question: what is master of my life?

p166.lead: A gospel that spreads without miracles: the Pharisees’ table at Ragaba, the Samaritan leper who returned, a new reading of the narrow door, accidents and providence, and Abner at Philadelphia.

p166.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p166.s0.h: Introduction — A Gospel Reflecting His Teachings More Than His Personality
p166.s0.b0: From February 11 to 20, Jesus and the twelve toured the cities and villages of northern Perea where Abner’s associates and the women’s corps were at work. They found the messengers succeeding, and Jesus repeatedly called the apostles’ attention to the fact that the gospel of the kingdom could spread without miracles and wonders.
p166.s0.b1: The text says that this three-month mission succeeded with little help from the twelve, and that from this time on the gospel reflected his teachings more than his personality. But his followers did not keep to this direction for long. After his death and resurrection they built the early church around miraculous concepts and glorified memories of his personality.
p166.s1.h: I. The Pharisees at Ragaba — The Outside and the Inside of the Cup
p166.s1.b0: On the Sabbath of February 18, Nathaniel, a wealthy Pharisee of Ragaba, invited Jesus as guest of honor to a breakfast together with some twenty fellow Pharisees who had been following the tour. Jesus sat down at once without washing his hands at the basin. He washed only for cleanliness and greatly disliked purely ceremonial acts. The host was shocked, and those across the table sneered and twisted their mouths.
p166.s1.b1: Jesus observed that they had invited him in order to display their ceremonial devotion to their own righteousness, and then he rebuked a religion whose outside and inside did not match. He first acknowledged that many Pharisees were his friends and even his disciples, but he made it plain that God looks not at outward piety but at the inner motives of the soul.
p166.s1.b3: When a lawyer complained that these words reproached his class too, Jesus rebuked the lawyers who load heavy burdens on people without lifting a finger and take away the key of knowledge. Yet he said that the doors of the kingdom of heaven are open to all who have faith and will not be shut by the prejudice and arrogance of false teachers. He left the house without eating.

Jesus’ response on this occasion

2. Scrupulous observance of the laws of purification

3. Avoiding fellowship with non-Pharisees

p166.s1.b6: Some of the Pharisees who heard him believed and entered the kingdom, but more of them hardened their resolve to catch him in words they could use against him. The same words became a door to some and a stumbling block to others.
p166.s2.h: II. The Ten Lepers — A Stranger’s Gratitude
p166.s2.b0: Near Amathus, Jesus met ten lepers. Nine were Jews and one a Samaritan; their common suffering had carried them past religious prejudice. Jesus happened to be explaining why the gentiles and less orthodox Jews of Perea were more ready to believe the gospel, yet the apostles were still reluctant to feel kindly toward Samaritans.
p166.s2.b1: Simon Zelotes suggested they pass by, since a Samaritan was among them. Jesus answered that the Samaritan might prove more grateful than the Jews, and asked whether they should sit in judgment on their fellows. Then he told the ten to go and show themselves to the priests, and on the way they were all made whole.
p166.s2.b4: As the Samaritan left, all the apostles looked at Jesus except Simon Zelotes, who hung his head. No one spoke, and Jesus said nothing; there was no need. The text adds that only four of the ten actually had leprosy, the other six having a skin disease, and that the Samaritan was a true leper.
p166.s2.b5: Jesus explained the event as the difference between the children of the house and the stranger. The children take their blessings for granted and neglect to give thanks, while the stranger, filled with wonder at the gift, cannot help being grateful. The insight that gratitude dulls the longer grace is received speaks with special sharpness to those who live amid long habits of faith.
p166.s3.h: III. The Sermon at Gerasa — The Narrow Door Is Wide Enough for All
p166.s3.b0: Asked whether few or many would be saved, Jesus first reviewed the ideas then current: the teaching that only the children of Abraham would be saved, the notion that just as few of those who left Egypt reached the promised land, so only a few would enter the kingdom, and the proverb of the narrow door and the broad way. He granted that the proverb held truth, but he gave it a new interpretation.
p166.s3.b2: The danger lies not in the size of the door but in delay. For those who pursue immature pleasures and selfishness, refusing to enter the spiritual experience, and then knock later to be counted among the great when the glory is revealed, the door is shut. But all who sincerely seek will surely find eternal salvation, and people will come from every direction to possess the kingdom by living faith.
